h1: SEO in Jodhpur for furniture exporters selling to America
metaTitle: SEO Services in Jodhpur: Furniture and Handicraft Export
metaDescription: Jodhpur exporters are found by US and EU wholesale buyers, not by neighbours. We build the container-load and catalogue content those buyers search for.
answer: Jodhpur runs India's largest wooden-handicraft furniture export cluster, and its buyers are American and European wholesalers searching in English for container-load terms — MOQ, CBM, FOB, lead time, 40-foot capacity. Most Jodhpur exporter websites never use those words, which is why the buyer finds them on Alibaba instead of on Google.
takeaways: Local SEO is irrelevant to a Jodhpur exporter. Your buyer is in Atlanta and will never type the word "Jodhpur".
Your competitors aren't other Jodhpur units. They're Alibaba, IndiaMART and Vietnamese suppliers with better English websites.
Publishing your MOQ will lose you enquiries — the ones you were going to decline anyway. That's the point.

sections.h2: Your buyer is in Atlanta, not in Jodhpur
body: Jodhpur is India's biggest wooden-handicraft furniture export cluster. Sheesham and mango wood, reclaimed timber, iron-and-wood industrial pieces, carved and painted work — trucked out through the dry port at Bhagat ki Kothi, containerised on to Mundra or Kandla, and shipped to importers and retail chains across the United States and Europe.

Which means almost none of your buyers will ever type the word "Jodhpur". They type "indian furniture manufacturer", "reclaimed wood furniture supplier", or the name of a style they photographed at a trade fair. Local SEO is irrelevant to you. This is an [international B2B search problem](/services/international-seo-services) that happens to be located in Rajasthan.

And the competitive field isn't the unit down the road in Boranada. It's Alibaba, IndiaMART, a handful of well-built exporter sites from Jodhpur and Saharanpur, and — increasingly — Vietnamese and Indonesian suppliers with better English websites than yours.

callout.title: Where the enquiry is actually lost
callout.body: Open a dozen Jodhpur exporter sites and you'll find most rank for their own company name and very little else. The buyer had already found them — at a fair, on a sourcing platform, through an agent — and came to the site to check whether the company was real. Then the site failed the check. Fix that page before you spend a rupee on rankings.

sections.h2: The vocabulary gap that costs you the enquiry
body: An American wholesale buyer sourcing furniture works from a specific vocabulary. It's in every RFQ they send and every filter they apply. Look at a typical Jodhpur exporter website and count how many of these words appear on it — the answer is usually one or two.
The left-hand column below is a keyword list nobody in Jodhpur targets. It's also the qualification questionnaire your sales team asks over email for three days. Put it on the page and you win both.

callout.title: The uncomfortable bit
callout.body: Stating your MOQ publicly will reduce your enquiry count. It removes the ones you were going to decline and the ones that were never going to close, and it raises the quality of what's left. Sales teams hate this suggestion and it works anyway.

sections.h2: Catalogue pages that survive a buyer's shortlist
body: A wholesale buyer builds a shortlist of five to ten suppliers and then eliminates. Your catalogue is where the elimination happens, and most Indian exporter catalogues are a PDF plus a photo grid with no text — so Google can't read them and the buyer can't filter them. Five fixes, in order of return.
numbered: **One indexable page per product family**, not per SKU. "Reclaimed wood dining tables" is a page. "RT-4471" is a row on it.

**Real text on every page**: dimensions in inches and centimetres, wood species, finish options, packing, CBM per piece, pieces per 40ft container. Each one is a filter a buyer applies before they email.
**Alt text that describes the product**, because much of this category's discovery starts in image search and on Pinterest rather than in a text query.

**Customisation described as a process.** "OEM welcome" means nothing. "We produce to your drawings; sampling takes 15–20 days; sample cost adjusted against the first order" means you've done it before.
**A page that proves you exist**: factory photographs with people in them, unit address, GST and IEC details, the fairs you exhibit at. This is the page that survives the check.

callout.title: Where the value actually lands
callout.body: You will never get thousands of visitors from this. You might get sixty a month from overseas buyers, and one of them places a container order. Judge the work on enquiry quality and order value — see [why rankings and traffic are the wrong scoreboard](/compare/keyword-rankings-vs-organic-traffic).

sections.h2: Guar gum and the other Jodhpur export
body: Jodhpur's other export story is guar. Rajasthan grows the bulk of India's guar, the Jodhpur–Bikaner belt processes it into splits and powder, and India supplies most of the world's guar gum — a large share into oilfield fracturing fluid, the rest into food and industrial grades.

The search behaviour is nothing like furniture. Guar buyers are industrial procurement teams searching by grade and specification: fast-hydrating, food grade, FCC compliant, viscosity in cP, mesh size, splits versus powder. And the market tracks North American drilling activity, which is why the price history has been so violent — the 2012 spike is still the reference point traders use.
bullets: Grade-level pages with real specification tables — viscosity, mesh, moisture, ash, protein. That table *is* the content strategy; everything else is packaging.
Certifications stated explicitly: FSSAI, Halal, Kosher, FCC compliance where it applies. These are search terms as well as trust signals.
Monthly capacity and packing, in metric tonnes and container loads. Same filter logic as furniture.
Don't build content around price forecasts you can't support. A wrong forecast is remembered longer than a right one.

sections.h2: Heritage hotels and destination weddings: a completely different search
body: The other half of Jodhpur's economy is visitors. Mehrangarh dominates the skyline and the search results, the blue quarter below it is among the most photographed places in India, and the palace-and-fort wedding market here is one of the country's strongest.
Wedding search breaks the normal SEO rules in two ways, and pretending otherwise is how agencies lose these accounts in month three.
bullets: **The research window runs six to eighteen months**, and the same person visits many times before enquiring. Brand search and returning visits are better progress signals than first-touch traffic, which makes month-one reporting close to meaningless.
**The decision is visual and social.** Instagram and Pinterest carry much of the discovery while Google carries the verification. Both need to exist; only one of them is SEO.
**Pricing is the query everyone hides.** "Destination wedding cost in Jodhpur" carries enormous intent and almost no honest content. A page with real ranges beats twelve pages of venue photography.
**Seasonality is fixed.** The season runs roughly October to March, and the searches that decide it happen months before. Publish and index accordingly.

body: SEO from ₹75,000 a month, and from ₹40,000 a month for smaller sites. Ex-GST, month-to-month after the first quarter, 30 days' notice, and you keep every page and login. Export work usually needs the ₹75,000 tier, because it means English written for a foreign reader, a real catalogue rebuild, and technical work on a site that was almost certainly built as a brochure.

The guarantee: we freeze your trailing-90-day count of qualified enquiries from organic search on day one, in writing, and if we haven't beaten it in 90 days we keep working free until we do. faqs.q: Do Jodhpur furniture exporters need local SEO?
faqs.a: Almost never. Your buyers are wholesalers in the US and Europe who will never search for a Rajasthan city. Keep a tidy Google Business Profile so you look real when someone checks, then put the entire budget into English product and capability content aimed at international buyers.

faqs.q: Should I publish my MOQ and prices on the website?
faqs.a: Publish MOQ, lead time and container capacity — always. They filter out enquiries you'd decline and pull in serious buyers. Prices are optional and often unwise on custom furniture, but publish a price band or a per-CBM indication if you can. A buyer with no cost signal at all moves to a supplier who gave one.

faqs.q: How much does SEO cost for a Jodhpur exporter?
faqs.a: We start at ₹75,000 a month for export engagements, ex-GST, because the work involves rebuilding the catalogue and writing for a foreign buyer rather than publishing blog posts. Smaller sites start at ₹40,000. Local Jodhpur providers quote far less and typically deliver directory submissions, which do nothing for an American buyer.

faqs.q: Is SEO better than Alibaba or IndiaMART for export enquiries?
faqs.a: It's different, not better, and you want both. Sourcing platforms give you volume and put you in a price fight with fifty identical listings. Your own site gives you fewer, better enquiries and a buyer who's already read your specifications. In practice most Jodhpur exporters use platforms for discovery and their website to close, so the website has to be worth arriving at.

faqs.q: How long does SEO take for an export business?
faqs.a: Specification and container-load terms can rank in 8–14 weeks because nobody in the cluster targets them. Broad category terms like "indian furniture manufacturer" take six months or more. Enquiries lag rankings because overseas buying cycles are long — expect the first traceable enquiry somewhere in months three to five, and a container order later than that.
